talks.title: 0x0A: Daniel Bohannon
talks.teaser: Explains how obfuscated PowerShell slips past common detections, and how feature-based scoring can flag it.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why common PowerShell detections miss attacks and how defenders can see through obfuscation. It opens with the logging that matters most, including command-line auditing and script block logging. It then walks through ways attackers launch PowerShell without a telling parent process or argument, such as piping commands through standard input, hiding payloads in environment variables, the clipboard or WMI, and renaming binaries. Download cradles are disguised with escape characters, case tricks, aliases and string manipulation, so the keywords a rule would match never appear in plain form.

To catch what simple indicators miss, the research team gathered about 408,000 public PowerShell scripts from 28,000 authors and labelled thousands of them by hand. A character-frequency baseline reached 89% precision and 37% recall. Extracting nearly 5,000 features from the syntax tree and weighting them with a linear model trained by gradient descent raised this to 96% precision, 94% recall and about 1% false positives. The talk also demonstrated a companion tool that scores scripts, rebuilds them from script block logs and supports whitelisting, with scoring taking less than 300 milliseconds per script.

The takeaway is to enable PowerShell 5 logging, look beyond process names and arguments, and hunt for obfuscated scripts alongside known indicators. The speaker acknowledged that a determined attacker could tune samples to evade the feature model, so results should be checked against each environment. The project was released openly so the community can contribute new samples and modifications.

talks.title: 0x0A: Carly Schneider
talks.teaser: Shows how Spotify built an open-source toolkit to inventory, scan and notify teams about misconfigured Google Cloud resources.
talks.summary:
A security engineer at Spotify explains why the company moved its infrastructure from its own data centers to Google Cloud and what that meant for security. With a small security team supporting thousands of engineers who own their own resources, the goal was visibility into cloud objects without blocking anyone's work. The team built First Eddie, an open-source modular toolkit for securing and monitoring Google Cloud resources, developed together with Google.

The architecture has four pipelines. An inventory snapshots Google Cloud resources into a Cloud SQL database each day. A scanner compares those objects against configurable rules and records violations. An enforcer automatically corrects violations, though at Spotify it is currently used only for firewall rules. A notifier emails the owning teams, and security is copied the next day if a problem remains. The talk covered three rule families: data storage exposure, such as openly shared BigQuery data, buckets and Cloud SQL instances; ownership rules that limit who can be added as an owner and which identities may own what; and network rules that watch external connections and firewall changes.

The speaker found that many violations came from engineers experimenting or from people with legitimate needs, and most fixed their issues after one friendly email. The main lesson was that notification volume must stay low, because an overloaded small team began muting alerts. Attendees were told the design could be adapted to other organizations, though porting it to other clouds would take considerable effort.

talks.title: 0x0A: Michael Goedeker - Snakeoil Factory Inc, risk intelligence and threat intelligence
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for 0x0A: Michael Goedeker - Snakeoil Factory Inc, risk intelligence and threat intelligence.

talks.title: 0x0A: Kyle Wilhoit
talks.teaser: A two-year case study separates media hype from the United Cyber Caliphate's real online tools, attacks, and intelligence gaps.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens on sensational news coverage of ISIS-linked hacking and poses whether such cyber terrorism matches the fear it generates. The speaker outlines a roughly two-year case study into groups often lumped under that label, distinguishing cyber terrorism (violence as the goal) from hacktivism (political access without violence as the primary aim).

The bulk of the talk maps the United Cyber Caliphate (UCC), formed when multiple ISIS-aligned factions merged, across media dissemination, fundraising including arms trafficking, and digital attacks. It surveys Facebook and Twitter use, Tor forums, Telegram channels, Android apps and magazines for propaganda and kinetic planning, weak homemade DDoS tools, defacements, simple SQL injection leaks presented as kill lists, and June-era malware built with a commodity builder tied to CVE-2016-0189. Poor operational security—open directories, image metadata, outdated encryption tools, and vBulletin forums—creates pivots for investigators even when attacks stay crude.

The closing argument is that UCC excels at information spread and recruitment and shows growing interest in OT, SCADA, and malware, but remains largely script-kiddie grade today. Practitioners should monitor those trajectories and exploit intelligence windows without accepting media narratives that every military network is already compromised.

talks.title: 0x0A: F1nux - The problem with other people’s tables
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in 0x0A: F1nux - The problem with other people’s tables.

talks.title: 0x0A: Mathias Karlsson
talks.teaser: Shows how a browser's legacy application cache can be abused to poison responses and steal signed S3 download links.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at offline caching in web browsers, where a site stores content locally so it stays viewable without a connection. Service workers are the modern option; the older Application Cache mechanism is the focus here. Its manifest file has cache, fallback and network sections. The key finding was that the fallback rule also fires when the server returns an error such as a 404 or 403, not only when the browser is offline.

Since same-domain uploads already imply deeper problems, the research looked at shared cloud storage. Anyone can create a bucket on Amazon S3, and applications often protect uploaded files with signed links. The attack places a crafted manifest in an attacker's bucket so that error responses fall back to attacker content. Signed URLs normally succeed, so the speaker sent a large number of oversized cookies to the browser, making requests fail. The poisoned cache then serves the attacker's file, which reveals the signature from the URL and allows download of a private file.

The speaker noted that browser vendors have responded unevenly. Chrome and Firefox have ported the path restriction that service workers use, while Internet Explorer declined to treat the issue as a security fix because Application Cache is deprecated, though it said a fix would come in a future release. The takeaway is that legacy browser features can reopen trust boundaries, so teams should check whether old caching behaviour overlaps with public storage and signed-URL protections.

talks.title: 0x0A: Olleb - Solving the Ceazars challenge 2016
talks.teaser: Walks through decoding a layered cipher puzzle, from digit-encoded text to substitution and transposition steps.
talks.summary:
The speaker revisits a puzzle from a past Caesars-themed challenge, working from a publicly posted image of coloured digits. Rather than starting from scratch, they show how the digits can be read in groups of three, which map to printable ASCII characters. Separating the colour layers exposes a welcome message in one colour, a credit to the challenge creators in another, and a third layer that initially looked like a rotated alphabet and was treated as a decoy.

The darker blue layer turns out to be a simple substitution cipher hiding a web address. The speaker uses repeated letter patterns, such as the HTTP prefix, to map a few letters, guesses a common top-level domain, and then runs a shell loop that tries candidate letters against DNS lookups, keeping only names that resolve. This leads to a site with two further cryptograms. One is a columnar transposition, where letters are arranged in five groups of five and the five-pointed star hint helps reveal a username containing "legion". The other is a phrase the organisers hinted would begin with "all"; the Legionnaire theme suggests a well-known saying, which the speaker enters without fully working through its cipher.

The walkthrough closes by submitting the username and phrase, with padding X characters removed, to reach a congratulations page. The main takeaway is that pattern analysis, thematic hints and automated lookups can together resolve a multi-stage challenge, even when one step is solved by context rather than by full decryption.

talks.title: 0x0A: Alex Radocea
talks.teaser: Reveals how iCloud Keychain syncing works and how OTR signature bugs could intercept secrets silently.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with Apple’s stated goals for iCloud Keychain: end-to-end encryption for credit cards, Wi‑Fi passwords, and autofill data across devices, plus recovery when hardware is lost. It contrasts public white-paper summaries with behavior found in Apple’s open-source code, including prior work from Via Forensics, Black Hat disclosures on HSM escrow, and Elcomsoft’s questions about two-factor authentication.

The core walkthrough covers recovery via HSM-backed escrow, SMS, and secure remote protocol, then focuses on syncing. Devices form a signed “circle of trust” through SOS Circle (ECDSA on secp256r1), while Off-the-Record messaging encrypts secret updates over iCloud’s key-value store. A hidden “cloud peer” not described in the white paper lets recovery add a device without booting others, because its private key can be escrowed.

The talk closes on offensive impact: a goto-fail-style bug in OTR signature verification that accepts roughly 32-byte crafted messages, enabling silent man-in-the-middle decryption without touching long-term identity keys, plus a stack-clash-style memory issue in the same area with harder reliability. The speaker argues similar flaws should have been caught after earlier Apple SSL bugs and calls for fuller protocol transparency.

talks.title: 0x0A: Lucas Lundgren - Using the iSCSI protocol to harvest unprotected hard drives
talks.teaser: Shows how unauthenticated iSCSI storage exposed online can be found, logged into and read or written.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at iSCSI, a protocol that lets remote clients attach disks over IP networks. The speaker explains that many internet-facing deployments had no authentication, so anyone who found an address could discover targets and log in. Using standard Windows and Linux initiator tools, he walked through discovery, login and mounting exposed volumes. His scanning was still running when the talk was given, and the count of exposed services rose over 2017.

Once a disk was attached, the file permissions set on the storage host no longer applied, so he could read and write the raw partitions directly. The material he described included corporate documents, internal schematics, scanned identity documents, databases and source code. He also found a ransomware note on some devices. Early fingerprinting pointed to QNAP and Synology as the most common vendors. He said he contacted affected owners, with mixed reactions.

For defenders, the advice was to restrict which addresses can reach iSCSI, enable CHAP authentication, and keep storage off the internet, including avoiding UPnP port mapping on routers. Nmap scripts can help find exposed iSCSI services on your own network. He noted that iSCSI offers little or no encryption and has not been audited in a long time, so exposure remains a real risk.

talks.title: 0x0A: Hugo Hirsh - Candy and competence
talks.teaser: Shows how candy, metrics, and broken-windows-style fixes help a security team build trust and pull non-technical staff into daily reporting.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with New York’s broken-windows policing in the early 1990s and the steep drop in murders and violent crime after petty offenses and environmental disorder were tackled aggressively. That story frames security work as going after small, visible failures before they normalize bigger risk.

From there it walks through standing up a security function: threat modeling assets versus actors (with a Batman example and a sparser corporate diagram), the insight that organizations must patch people as well as servers, and five lessons distilled from Rich Smith’s talk on effective security organizations—trust but verify, graph what moves, blameless post-mortems with five whys, reserving “no” for rare cases, and how one abrasive security person can collapse trust. Design thinking and build–measure–learn loops support shipping with security present from the start rather than bolting controls on late. Shadow IT becomes a signal of unmet needs; an internal reward program uses candy and leaderboards instead of cash across developers, lawyers, and physical-security observations, with regulators still a barrier to a full public bug bounty.

The close ties “broken windows” to expired certificates, propped doors, and viral internal tools with overbroad permissions—fixed in a more secure configuration rather than removed. Outreach, approachability, and positive reinforcement aim for steady tickets and desk visits; Q&A cites roughly two to three reports daily and recent early design sessions as signs the model is working.

talks.title: 0x0A: Arron 'f1nux' Finnon
talks.teaser: Traces privacy's history through architecture, law and religion, showing why it resists a clear definition.
talks.summary:
The talk traces the history of privacy and opens by showing how hard the concept is to define. Search results, quotes from lawyers and philosophers, and a remark from Vint Cerf that privacy may be an anomaly all fall short. The speaker suggests privacy is a cluster of related ideas, such as secrecy, intimacy and being private, that can exist separately from one another.

The middle section follows how living arrangements shaped expectations, from shared hearths and communal beds to chimneys that made internal walls possible and public bathing. It contrasts Roman and Greek house designs and looks at the Black Death's effect on sleeping arrangements. Legal cases show state intrusion: a 1361 English law targeted eavesdropping, while an 1844 scandal revealed that the Home Secretary had ordered Giuseppe Mazzini's mail intercepted. Mazzini proved it by sending test letters seeded with sand, poppy seeds and hair. Further examples include a Civil War request for telegraph taps, the panopticon prison design, and the move from public confession to private reflection once printed Bibles spread.

The closing part argues that the nothing-to-hide argument misses the point, since privacy is more than secrecy. The speaker notes that privacy protections usually arrive after exposure, citing the Equifax breach, and that technology and institutions keep pushing against each other. The talk ends by framing privacy as a direction rather than a destination, and offers a definition: the right to be human.

talks.summary: Benjamin Brown of Akamai CERT explains blockchain fundamentals for SEC-T listeners: distributed ledgers, consensus rules, peer-to-peer propagation, and why cryptocurrencies inherit both resilience and fraud risks. He contrasts centralized banking with decentralized nodes, notes scaling trade-offs where not every coin keeps full history, and sets up follow-on discussion of how criminals abuse exchanges and mixers. The interview tone is educational, aimed at operators who need vocabulary before threat-hunting blockchain abuse on Akamai-adjacent criminal infrastructure and Akamai-adjacent dark web underground markets.

talks.summary:
SEC-T's säkerhetspodcast interviews Michael Goedeker after his conference talk on threat and risk intelligence. He recounts growing up on Apple II and Commodore gear, UNIX ops work, and a career arc from classic hacking curiosity through incident response toward intelligence-driven defense products.

Goedeker contrasts checklist NIST incident handling with dynamic, automated correlation that still spends most analyst time on review but frees cycles for novel patterns. He advocates API-first collection using documented standards instead of brittle scrapers, feeding breach and indicator feeds into customer SIEMs with realistic expectations about probabilistic coverage rather than perfect attribution.

talks.title: 0x0A: Säkerhetspodcasten intervju Kyle Wilhoit
talks.teaser: Assesses whether self-styled cyber terrorist groups pose a real risk or mainly run propaganda, fundraising and recruitment.
talks.summary:
This interview with Kyle Wilhoit follows his talk on cyber terrorism. He begins with his background: he started programming at 13, holds computer science degrees, has worked only in security, and spent time in the intelligence community. His favourite hack is Stuxnet, because it bridged software and physical damage, and he points to a 2015 power outage in Ukraine as a clear real-world case of malware hitting operational technology.

He explains the research question: whether groups that call themselves cyber terrorists are a genuine threat. His conclusion is that much of their output is propaganda and public relations, with little real malware or information security capability so far, though the risk could grow if they adapt. He describes fundraising through money transfers and alternative currencies, and says some individuals who published propaganda also bought and sold weapons and body armour, including mortar rounds, on underground forums and onion sites. Where he finds information such as drop servers, he passes it to government entities, including those of the country being targeted.

The discussion then turns to the dilemmas facing researchers. Taking sites down may stop an attack but ends monitoring that can reveal wider infrastructure, so he sees each case as a judgement call. He also weighs how much to publish, since disclosure can teach adversaries to improve their operational security. Practitioners should take away that the threat is still largely propaganda, that monitoring and disclosure need careful balance, and that the picture may change over time.

talks.title: 0x0A: Säkerhetspodcasten intervju Zoz Brooks
talks.teaser: Explores destroying hard-drive data in sixty seconds, safety around explosives, and rumors of intelligence recovery from crushed disks.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens as a break-time interview with someone who just presented on physically destroying data, framed around a challenge to wipe a hard drive in about sixty seconds while keeping the method contained. The guest describes a casual path into hacking as curiosity about how systems work, then reflects on phone phreaking, high-impact physical hacks such as hotel electronic locks, and showy safe-opening demos as examples of clever, low-tech brilliance.

Most of the discussion returns to that destruction talk: inspiration from an earlier conference presentation, motivations tied to explosives industry contacts and interest in three-dimensional printing energetic materials, and experiments run with bomb-squad supervision in Colorado. The guest recounts Mythbusters-style trials, thermite and high-explosive work behind earth berms and vehicles, and protecting high-speed cameras worth tens of thousands of dollars while still capturing dramatic footage, including material originally shot for a television segment on extreme high-voltage effects.

The middle and end pivot to forensic reality versus intelligence recovery. Second-hand stories suggest agencies may still want storage that was only crushed or cut, not also burned, while the guest argues platter deformation makes civilian recovery nearly implausible though nation-state budgets could change the calculus. Personal risk tolerance, future recovery technology, and conventional forensic limits on damaged platters round out what practitioners should weigh before trusting a single nail or shredder pass.

SEC-T podcasts interview Arron "f1nux" Finnon after his keynote on privacy, governments, and surveillance, tracing his path from mature web developer to Scotland's first undergraduate ethical-hacking degree and his pivot from attack traffic generation to philosophical data work. Finnon argues privacy is a physiological need whose violation measurably stresses humans, walks through historical shifts from intentional eavesdropping norms to always-on cameras and social media exposure, and compares Swedish publicity laws with U.S. Fourth Amendment fruits-of-the-poisonous-tree doctrine.

The conversation roams across Equifax awakening public anger, teenage oversharing versus learned helplessness, Apple Face ID consent, forensic access to cached cloud sessions on seized laptops, and whether technology alone can restore privacy before exposure rather than after breaches. Finnon urges education and pre-exposure design over reactive regulation while acknowledging governments and corporations keep expanding collection capabilities.

talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning 0x0A: Säkerhetspodcasten intervju Hanno Böck.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Hanno Böck, a security researcher, discusses findings from his investigation into accidental file exposure and wget-based vulnerabilities discovered through web misconfigurations. The interview takes place at Säkerhetspodcasten's 10th anniversary event, with host Midori.

## Key Topics

**The wget Investigation**
Böck explains how his research began when two people contacted him regarding wget vulnerabilities—specifically, the ability to download directories from web pages deployed with wget. This observation sparked deeper investigation into related configuration and file exposure issues.

**MySQL Dumps and Database Access**
A critical finding involves MySQL database dumps being left in web roots with standard filenames (such as dump.sql) from the documentation. These are easily discoverable and downloadable by attackers. Server logs showed others attempting to download such files, suggesting the vulnerability was known informally but never publicly discussed in articles or blog posts.

**PHP Core Dumps**
When PHP applications crash, the system can generate core dumps (memory dumps) in the web root depending on configuration. These dumps contain sensitive information, particularly database passwords stored in variables. While Böck found PHP crashes are common corner cases that developers don't prioritize fixing, he has not found a reliable way to remotely trigger crashes consistently.

**Magento Configuration Vulnerability**
Magento stores configuration in XML files containing database passwords. Unlike PHP files (which are parsed and protected), XML files are plain text and downloadable. While Magento uses .htaccess restrictions, this only works on Apache; nginx deployments require manual configuration. When reported through Magento's bug bounty program, the company indicated the issue was already known but provided no timeline for fixes.

**Research Methodology**
Böck scanned the Alexa top 1 million websites to assess prevalence. He considered certificate transparency logs as an alternative for broader domain discovery but chose the limited scope to avoid abuse concerns. When informing affected organizations, he contacts abuse contacts—not an ideal use of responsible disclosure channels, but effective.

**Artifacts and Misconfigurations**
The research reveals that web roots contain unintended files including old configuration files, swap files, and backup artifacts. These emerge from development processes or abandoned domains.

## Key Findings

Böck emphasizes that while individual customers responded positively when notified (removing exposed files), the Magento vulnerability in particular received minimal public attention. However, a German article generated significant media impact in Germany, including coverage of issues with the German Postal Service's systems.

The speaker released tools to facilitate scanning, expressing dissatisfaction with the limited availability of public vulnerability scanning tools for these issues. He notes that as frameworks mature and domains are abandoned, JavaScript inclusion attacks and other configuration-based vulnerabilities will likely increase.

## Takeaways

The research demonstrates that sensitive files routinely end up in web roots through misconfiguration, developer shortcuts, or inadequate understanding of web server behavior across different platforms. While individual organizations can remediate when notified, systematic change requires greater public awareness and better default security practices. Böck hopes releasing scanning tools will improve the overall security posture.

talks.title: 0x09 SEC-T Community night: Mattias Borg
talks.teaser: A practitioner shares recorded tech-support scam calls, counter-scam tactics, and paths to report call centers effectively.
talks.summary:
Mattias Borg describes a deliberately non-technical community talk focused on telephone tech-support scams. He opens by urging security practitioners to share knowledge more widely, then outlines his side interest in social engineering and human-focused security.

He walks through baiting scammers who claimed to be from Microsoft, including staging a VM, following their Run dialog and remote-access instructions, and observing fake “hacked services” and Event Viewer proof. He renamed analysis tools on the guest machine without the caller noticing, reacted to on-screen intimidation text about licensing and infection percentages, and eventually regained control when a second victim appeared in the same remote session. A brief outreach call to another person tied to credentials visible during the session illustrates how victims overlap.

He closes with practical limits on illegal retaliation, advocacy that helped extend Microsoft’s scam-reporting to Sweden after a wave targeting Swedish citizens, and the point that awareness and common sense matter as much as technical controls. He invites analysts to review published capture material and report findings.

talks.title: 0x09 SEC-T Community night: Olleb
talks.teaser: A live PCAP and Python client walkthrough cracks layered XOR, ANSI clues, and RC4 keystream reuse to rebuild a hidden game session.
talks.summary:
The session walks through a spring recruitment-style puzzle built around a PCAP capture and a Python game client. The challenge readme asks for visual details—a ball color, playing field, colors, and the top high score—while the capture holds mostly opaque TCP payloads plus routine HTTP. The presenter uses Wireshark’s protocol hierarchy and TCP stream following to pull out the client, then patches it to replay saved streams instead of talking to a live socket.

Progress moves through stacked encoding layers. A single-byte XOR gate is validated with MD5 and yields early plaintext; a repeating twelve-byte XOR key is inferred from pattern analysis and ANSI terminal framing, with plaintext hints tied to a classic breakout-style game and a 1987 release year. The last stage misuses RC4: one key, no per-message IV, so every ciphertext shares the same keystream. Unique RC4 blobs are extracted, lengths tied to a growing high-score table, and known player names plus score text serve as cribs. Sliding those guesses across misaligned messages recovers keystream slices and decrypts the scoreboard—including a 1000-point run—until the submission address appears.

The takeaway for practitioners is how network forensics, light reversing, and classical stream-cipher mistakes chain together in one artifact. The talk stresses puzzle craft over hiring, but the methods mirror real weaknesses: custom protocols in PCAP, XOR and RC4 deployed without proper key handling, and crib-based attacks when the same keystream encrypts related UI updates.

talks.title: 0x09 SEC-T Community night: Fredrik Söderblom, Joachim Strömbergsson & Peter Norin
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in 0x09 SEC-T Community night: Fredrik Söderblom, Joachim Strömbergsson & Peter Norin.
talks.summary:
SEC-T community night presenters revisit a large star-topology customer audit spanning hundreds of remote sites with parallel data, alarm, and video links. XPD consultants describe how odd centralized-to-branch routing created unexpected exposure points and why geographically dispersed greenfield rollouts need holistic reviews beyond the data VLAN everyone worries about first.

Speakers share Swedish embedded-security war stories, emphasize crypto reviews on alarm and CCTV paths, and argue star hubs magnify blast radius when one concentrator misroutes traffic or trusts the wrong WAN peers.

talks.title: 0x08: Alec - Breaking bricks and plumbing pipes
talks.teaser: Shows how a Cisco ASA firewall can be taken over and used to blend malicious traffic into the expected network.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the idea that a firewall is the trust anchor of a network, so owning it lets an attacker shape traffic to match what the rule base expects. The speaker, a firewall engineer new to Cisco ASA, bought a cheap legacy 5505 appliance and found that it runs the same firmware as larger models. Its Linux environment exists only to launch the firewall process, and the legacy firmware checks its embedded hashes only after upload, not at boot. That gap allows a modified image to persist, with a kernel module hiding the altered file and a reverse shell routed through a hidden SOCKS proxy.

The middle of the talk covers reaching the device from the internet. A command injection in a configuration setting gives a shell without a reboot. A directory traversal in the web VPN customization preview bypasses the session check, so an attacker can plant a fake login page, capture credentials and reuse a session cookie to open a VPN. A version leak helped locate targets, and the failover link accepted unauthenticated proprietary packets that ran commands and replaced configuration on the standby unit without logging. Malicious NAT rules then made traffic appear to come from expected hosts, and a ptrace-based patch hid those rules from the administrator.

The takeaway is that firewalls are software with a growing attack surface and should be hardened like any server. Disable unused services, restrict management access and apply the patches Cisco has released.

talks.title: 0x08: Colin
talks.teaser: Shows how power measurements and glitches let attackers pull secret keys and bypass checks in embedded devices.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces physical attacks on hardware such as embedded devices, smart cards and security modules, using open-source hardware and software. The speaker stresses that these attacks only work once you understand how the target is built and which algorithm it runs. He starts with simple timing leaks: a PIN checker that exits early on a wrong digit reveals how many digits were correct, and a bootloader that hangs on a bad password still leaks through its power draw.

Next comes power analysis. Measuring supply current through a small resistor or with a magnetic field probe works because switching data lines draw power in proportion to the number of set bits. Using that model, differential power analysis recovers an AES key one byte at a time from a few dozen traces, shown in a live demo. A second case targets an AES-256 bootloader that decrypts attacker-supplied firmware, where the key and initialization vector were recovered from roughly 120 decryptions. Another example is an 802.15.4 radio node whose hardware AES engine leaks its key after about 10,000 messages, with the device still answering normal traffic throughout.

The final part covers voltage glitching against a Raspberry Pi and an Android phone, where brief power drops skip loop iterations in user-space code and corrupt results. The talk closes with trigger techniques and the open-source ChipWhisper hardware and software, with documentation that lets engineers test their own devices and check vendor claims.

talks.title: 0x08: Finux - The wrong side of history
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning 0x08: Finux - The wrong side of history.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this non-technical presentation on ethics and politics in technology, the speaker draws extensive parallels between the historical Manhattan Project and contemporary global surveillance programs exposed by Edward Snowden. By examining how fear-driven weaponization, extreme compartmentalization, whistleblowers, and escalating arms races defined the nuclear era, the speaker argues that modern computer scientists and cybersecurity professionals occupy a role analogous to the theoretical physicists of the 1940s. The talk warns against repeating history and challenges researchers to consider the real-world applications of their work.

### Key Topics
- **Historical Parallels in Secrecy and Whistleblowing:** The speaker compares Edward Snowden's revelations of PRISM and global surveillance to Klaus Fuchs, the physicist who leaked nuclear secrets from the Manhattan Project to the Soviet Union out of ideological conviction rather than financial gain.
- **Origins Driven by Fear:** Both projects originated from acute fear of adversaries. The Manhattan Project was initiated following Einstein's warning to Roosevelt about German nuclear capabilities, despite subsequent intelligence showing Nazi research was far behind what was feared.
- **Compartmentalization and Infrastructure:** A vast apparatus (employing over 110,000 workers at sites like Chicago and Los Alamos under General Leslie Groves) operated with only a fraction of personnel understanding the end product, mirroring large-scale modern defense and intelligence operations.
- **The German U-234 Cargo:** The talk recounts the capture of German submarine U-234 en route to Japan, whose cargo of uranium oxide (U-235) was seized by the United States, enriched, and ultimately incorporated into weapons dropped on Japan.
- **The Nuclear and Cyber Arms Races:** Oppenheimer opposed the development of thermonuclear weapons engineered by Edward Teller, recognizing they lacked strategic restraint and would trigger an endless escalation. The speaker links this to modern cyber warfare, the stockpile of zero-day vulnerabilities, and state-sponsored offensive intelligence budgets exceeding global defensive spending.

### Technical Details
- **Weapons and Implosion Mechanics:** The presentation contrasts the untested "Little Boy" gun-type uranium mechanism with the "Fat Man" implosion device tested at the Trinity site, noting that British expertise with shaped charges from Normandy proved crucial in making the plutonium core implode uniformly.
- **Thermal Expansion Mishap at Trinity:** During assembly in the desert, thermal expansion caused the plutonium core to initially not fit inside the device casing until ambient temperatures equalized after several hours.
- **Offensive vs. Defensive Spending Disparity:** Drawing on 2014 metrics, the speaker highlights that the U.S. spent approximately $52.6 billion on intelligence (with roughly 80% allocated to contractors), whereas total worldwide cybersecurity defense spending stood at around $40 billion.
- **Surveillance and Targeting:** The speaker points to metadata being used operationally (such as drone strikes in Pakistan) and the mass compromise of global cellular networks for SIM card encryption keys as evidence that digital research directly impacts real-world physical security.

### Takeaways
- **Research Consequences:** Security researchers must recognize that discovery and tool creation do not happen in a vacuum; capabilities developed for analysis or testing can be repurposed into offensive state weapons.
- **Modern McCarthyism:** Parallels are drawn between Cold War-era investigations (including Oppenheimer's revoked clearance) and the modern criminalization or vilification of hackers and transparency activists like Aaron Swartz.
- **Ethical Choice in Cybersecurity:** The speaker concludes that practitioners face a definitive ethical crossroads: deciding whether their talents will be dedicated to building intercept and offensive surveillance tools or engineering stronger defense and encryption.

talks.title: 0x08: Fredrik - The Cryptech project is awesome
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in 0x08: Fredrik - The Cryptech project is awesome.
talks.summary: Fredrik presents the Cryptech open HSM effort aimed at trustworthy randomness and tamper-aware key storage for operators who cannot audit black-box commercial modules. He walks through avalanche-noise entropy on FPGAs, whitening pitfalls seen via chi-square tooling, and the alpha board that pairs ARM cores with true RNG blocks bound for DNSSEC-style deployments. Snowden praise and crowd skepticism about openness frame why the team publishes BSD-licensed designs and invites third-party review instead of selling finished appliances. Demo boards, Novena bring-up, and comparisons to hobby Raspberry Pi TRNG projects illustrate how open hardware can still chase nation-state assurance goals.

talks.title: 0x08: Kalle - The way the cookie crumbles
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding 0x08: Kalle - The way the cookie crumbles.
talks.summary:
Kalle explores how the Same-Origin Policy fails against creative cookie and CSRF attacks even when enterprises deploy WAFs or X-Frame-Options. He demonstrates SQL injection chains that exfiltrate data via blind timing in cross-origin iframes, then shows session fixation and sibling-domain cookie injection that let attackers plant session cookies before victims authenticate.

Browsers emit every matching cookie without indicating order, so prepended malicious values can win. He critiques appliance CSRF tokens that only protect HTML forms, notes HttpOnly does not stop overwriting cookies, and urges global CSRF tokens plus binding authentication cookies to application session IDs to defeat fixation and split-session attacks in enterprises running separate auth and app cookies.. Live demos include famous leaked password sets recovered purely through browser-side timing without direct database access.

talks.title: 0x08: Marion
talks.teaser: Rates seven malware case studies, from Zeus to Cheshire Cat, on eight traits that make reverse engineering harder.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a reverse engineer, argues that the line between mass malware and targeted malware is blurring, and that labels such as advanced persistent threat say little about how a binary is built. Rather than judging samples by their victims or operators, the talk proposes a complexity scale built on eight traits, using Stuxnet as the top benchmark without analysing its binaries.

Seven case studies are placed on the scale. Zeus is presented as a long-lived banking trojan whose leaked source spawned many variants, making it successful rather than sophisticated. Sality, a polymorphic file infector, is noted for a botnet controlled by infected machines themselves. Black POS, which scraped card data from retail point-of-sale memory, is shown as simple code. Havex, which used the OPC interface to gather information on industrial control servers, sits in the middle, as do Babar and Evil Bunny; Evil Bunny uses embedded Lua scripts to change its behaviour at runtime. Cheshire Cat, active against old Windows systems and cautious about network noise, ranks highest alongside Evil Bunny.

The eight traits cover binary uniqueness, update frequency, repeated artifacts such as reused servers or file names, environment checks, multiple persistence methods, layered evasion, modular design and use of unusual execution spaces. Examples include varying compiler settings, building strings at runtime, and date checks that keep sandboxes from seeing behaviour. For defenders, the takeaway is that reused infrastructure and fixed artifacts are where analysts tend to gain ground.

talks.title: 0x08: Olle
talks.teaser: Security researchers investigate 0x08: Olle and analyze defensive countermeasures.

talks.title: 0x08: Oona - Scraping poorly redacted id cards on Instagram
talks.teaser: Shows how blurred ID photos posted on Instagram can still expose national identity numbers encoded in a barcode.
talks.summary:
Oona starts with a driver's licence photo that someone posted on Instagram, and a hashtag that gathered hundreds of similar posts. In Finland the personal identity code printed on a licence works as an identifier, so a name plus that code can be enough for some services to be misused, for example to open accounts or take out fast loans. The speaker explains that the same number is also encoded in a Code 39 barcode on the card, and that this barcode is easy to read when the image is sharp and aligned to the pixel grid.

Many of the posts were low resolution, or the barcode had been blurred or partly covered. The speaker argues that blur behaves like a low-pass filter rather than random noise, so it can be modelled and partly reversed by testing candidate values. Using OpenCV, a custom C++ reader locks onto the thick start and stop markers, samples the bars, and uses the regular white lines between characters to synchronise. A further technique shrinks the image to a single pixel row and scales it back up, which brings out the edges of the digits. Where a digit was covered, a brute-force script tried the possible combinations and kept the ones that passed the check digit.

The closing point is that the redaction in these posts was incomplete: the printed number was often hidden while the barcode was left untouched. The talk is a hobby project, and the takeaway is that partial blurring is weak protection for identifiers, and that people should not publish identity documents at all.

talks.title: 0x08: Säkerhetspodcasten
talks.teaser: Panel of podcast hosts debate ethics of exploit research, disclosure pressure, and the security risks of connected devices.
talks.summary:
This live recording from the SEC-T conference is a podcast-style panel in which the hosts answer questions sent in by the audience, some through a social media hashtag and some from people in the room. The first major theme is the ethics of vulnerability research. The panel weighs whether researchers can control how their findings are used, whether building exploits for law enforcement can be justified, and how much say security professionals have over where their work ends up.

The discussion then turns to disclosure. Panelists describe cases where vendors answered researchers with legal threats rather than fixes, and they argue that a public demonstration is sometimes the only way to get a company to act. They point to recent car hacking work and to an aircraft security claim as examples, and they note that offensive research carries a reputation problem that makes it look more exciting than defensive work.

Looking ahead, the group expects connected devices, from appliances to aircraft and vehicles, to repeat old mistakes such as weak input handling and poor configuration, with cheap devices becoming pivot points into larger networks. They agree that locked-down devices will get harder to exploit but will never be unhackable. Their closing point is that the industry should stop relying on perimeter walls and should build security into products from the start.

talks.title: 0x08: Travis and Sergey - A protocol for Leibowitz
talks.teaser: Explores covert channels in HF digital modes by abusing parser differences between radio receivers.
talks.summary:
The presentation ties amateur HF digital radio to parser differentials and hidden messaging, using A Canticle for Leibowitz as a metaphor for preserving knowledge when public infrastructure fails. Operating under rules that permit personal traffic but not cryptography, it shows how RTTY and PSK31 can carry a second story while on-air chatter stays mundane.

On RTTY, shift sequences and idle tones let Cyrillic text slip past standard Latin gear; on PSK31, extra idle zeros and overlong codewords bury data that eavesdroppers’ decoders discard. The speakers combine orthogonal modulation dimensions so one signal serves PSK31, Morse, and RTTY at once, and exploit mismatched receiver logic—such as treating amplitude dips as zero bits—to XOR disagreements into a covert channel. They revisit abusing forward error correction in weak-signal protocols and invite tooling to separate deliberate bit damage from noise.

The closing thread covers unintended 10-meter-band interference from Ethernet load, timing-shaped traffic as a remote “Madeline” exfiltration channel, and an over-the-air capture-the-flag concept without the public internet. The takeaway is to treat radio receivers as state machines worth reverse engineering, master simple modes before complex wireless stacks, and stay courteous on the bands so experiments do not attract hostile attention.

talks.title: 0x08: Vogelfrei - An introduction to covert communications with APRS
talks.teaser: Explains how the amateur radio APRS protocol's open design can be bent into a covert communication channel.
talks.summary:
APRS is an amateur radio protocol for sharing position and short status messages over a shared radio channel. The talk describes it as stateless, with no enforced authority: callsigns come from licensing, the passcode algorithm is public, and nothing stops a station from impersonating another. Packets are plain ASCII frames relayed through internet gateways, and public feeds expose the position reports, so activity is easy to follow.

The middle of the talk looks at ways the format can carry hidden data. Third-party and user-defined packets allow arbitrary content, and an encrypted payload can be placed in a packet body using a pre-shared key, though the packet format still makes such traffic easy to spot. The speaker also covers implementation quirks in gateway software, which are often less careful than the specification, and abuse of telemetry extensions and position ambiguity fields. Legal limits on encrypted amateur transmissions are noted, along with how direction finding and transmitter fingerprinting can reveal a station.

The closing takeaway is that amateur radio's safety rests on good faith rather than enforcement, so practitioners should read the implementations instead of trusting the spec. Demonstrations were kept brief, and the speaker mentioned a software modem and a Python library as work in progress.

talks.title: 0x07: Sergey Bratus - For want of a nail
talks.teaser: Traces simple parser bugs behind Heartbleed, Apple goto fail and Android master key flaws, and argues for grammar-faithful input parsing.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at a run of avoidable parser bugs from 2013 and 2014, several of which were nominated for or won a pony bounty. The speaker argues that these failures come from input formats that are context-sensitive, with dependent length fields and redundant values, being handled by ad hoc parsers that mix validity checks with memory allocation, copying and branching. Older cases such as BIND, OpenSSH and an OpenBSD ICMPv6 bug are presented as the same pattern.

Several recent cases are walked through in turn. In Heartbleed, the missing check was that two length fields in a heartbeat message agree, so the server echoed back more data than the request contained. In Apple's goto fail, a duplicated line caused a validity check to be skipped. The Android master key issue came from one component verifying a signed package's zip contents while another, using unsigned integers in C++, unpacked different contents. Apache and Nginx both had chunked-encoding size bugs, where a large hex value could be read as negative, with the same flaw surfacing in Nginx eleven years after Apache's fix.

The practical takeaway is to fully recognize and validate input before processing it, keep message formats as simple as possible, and write parsers whose code mirrors the grammar so auditors can see the structure. The speaker presents the Hammer parser-combinator library as one route toward that and points to the LangSec community for further work.

talks.title: 0x07: Travis Goodspeed
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding 0x07: Travis Goodspeed - A neighborly surprise talk.
talks.summary:
Travis Goodspeed demonstrates active disk anti-forensics and weaponized hard-drive backdoors spanning iPod disk mode, Rockbox firmware hooks, and reversed Seagate firmware. His FaceDancer USB work fingerprints forensic imaging versus normal reads, then serves Rick Astley lyrics or erases evidence once dd-style sequential scans trip hidden sectors.

The Seagate project with collaborators fingerprints hosts via SCSI quirks, injects GDB stubs into drive ARM cores, and exfiltrates database blocks by rewriting MySQL records from inside the disk without touching the server OS. He urges readers to reproduce PoC||GTFO papers, warns inline USB sniffers may be the only general detection, and notes damaged-sector remaps preserve overwritten secrets. Goodspeed declines on-stage questions so attendees swap tricks in the hallway instead. SEC-T hosts this as their recurring hardware horror slot.

talks.title: 0x07: Mattias Karlsson
talks.teaser: Shows how a payload abuses JavaScript prototype and sort internals to escape the AngularJS template sandbox and run XSS.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces AngularJS, a JavaScript framework that evaluates double-curly-brace template expressions before rendering the page. These expressions run inside a sandbox that blocks access to dangerous objects such as window and document, so a simple injected alert fails. The problem is that AngularJS decodes HTML-entity-encoded templates before executing them, which makes a sandbox escape the key risk for applications that rely on that encoding for protection.

The speaker then walks through a bypass. Because direct access to the Function constructor is blocked, the payload creates an array and sorts it using the Function constructor as the comparison function, which produces a function that runs outside the sandbox in the global scope. Next, it overrides the prototype toString method with Function.prototype.call, so that when the engine compares that function with an integer, it converts the function to a string and ends up executing the code. The end result is an alert that fires despite the sandbox.

According to the speaker, this technique worked on almost every AngularJS application at the time. A fix had been released in a newer version of the framework only shortly before the talk. The practical takeaway is to update affected AngularJS applications to the patched release and to stop treating the template sandbox as a reliable barrier against cross-site scripting.

talks.title: 0x07: Olle Segerdahl
talks.teaser: Covers how to pick storage encryption by key handling, tamper properties, and threat models—not bit counts or marketing labels.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by dismantling common storage-encryption marketing: AES bit lengths, NIST or CSE hardware certifications, and vague “military-grade” claims do not tell buyers whether a product fits their needs. Encryption is framed as shrinking the secret users must protect from vast data volumes down to a small key, which makes key management the decisive factor—where keys are created, stored, used, and shielded from unauthorized access, including how PIN or password authentication relates to the underlying cipher strength.

Midway, the speaker contrasts threat scenarios: recovering a laptop or drive lost in a taxi versus leaving a machine in a hotel room while dining imposes different attacker motivation, skill, and convenience tradeoffs. Software full-disk encryption often weakens on tampering and boot trust; stronger protection against determined adversaries typically adds authentication and tamper-check steps. Built-in full-disk encryption on major operating systems is a reasonable baseline, but dedicated USB or external products demand clearer loss-scenario thinking before purchase.

The close urges professional evaluation mapped to those scenarios—not binary “secure or not” answers—and, for public-sector audiences, possible support from MSB. Deployments should include user procedures for real incidents, such as recovery-key prompts or a lost laptop in a taxi, so operational response matches the technical control.

talks.title: 0x07: Anna Shubina
talks.teaser: Fingerprinting VPNs explores 0x07: Anna Shubina.

talks.title: 0x07: Marta Janus
talks.teaser: Maps a decade of SOHO router threats, including drive-by farming, router botnets, firmware backdoors, and cross-platform IoT worms.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames small home routers and ADSL modems as long-standing targets for online crime, building on a 2011 threat-landscape study the author published on Securelist. Default SNMP and UPnP exposure, unchanged community strings, and protocols many owners never know exist create easy footholds. Large-scale DNS redirection—drive-by or SOHO farming—replaces resolver settings so victims reach phishing sites; campaigns reached millions of users across Brazil, Mexico, Europe, the United States, and Asia.

The middle of the talk walks through router botnets and evolving abuse. Early binary malware on routers (for example Psybot, reported at roughly 880,000 infected devices in 2009, and later Chuck Norris targeting D-Link and Linksys via authentication bypass) showed obfuscation and reinfection after reboot until firmware was fixed. By 2014 several 2011 predictions had already landed: more firmware flaws, hardcoded backdoors such as one triggered by a specific browser user-agent string, continued SOHO farming (including attacks on Polish banks and later reports of more than 300,000 affected devices in India, Vietnam, and Italy), multi-architecture worms (ARM, MIPS, x86) acting as IoT malware with remote shell and cryptocurrency mining plugins, script-based persistent firmware overwrite, the Moon worm, and Black Energy pushing ARM ELF modules to home routers for DDoS.

The closing argument is that sophistication and scale are outpacing defenses. Media attention and some vendor and ISP outreach have grown, yet there is no universal mitigation, and non-technical users rarely apply updates on old hardware. Practitioners are left to keep finding issues responsibly, widen awareness among vendors, and accept that abandoned devices remain exposed.

talks.title: 0x07: Hugo Teso
talks.teaser: Presents aviation attack vectors through airline ground services and avionics software updates, with exploit details withheld.
talks.summary:
Hugo Teso returns to update his earlier aviation security research, arguing that the industry should treat security as distinct from safety. The recap covers his previous attack chain: mapping aircraft with ADS-B, listening to the plain-text ACARS datalink to identify onboard systems by their database formats, and then reaching aircraft through the web portals of ground service providers, where web flaws could expose user credentials that allowed sending messages.

The new work starts with how an outsider might get hold of the software that aircraft load. Ordering an airline media set from a vendor led him to a wireless loading product that pushes airline-modifiable information to aircraft over cellular or Wi-Fi links. He said more than a hundred operators use it, and it can reach more than a dozen onboard systems, including the flight management system. To study the code, he used a training simulator that shares source with the real system, ran it in an old VxWorks development environment with simulated avionics inputs, and found a parsing flaw that crashed the flight management system.

He closed with a drone project in which a real flight management system controlled a small drone over a telemetry link. Some test runs worked, while others left the drone losing control. His main point is that entry barriers are low: public websites, free tools and firmware updates are enough to start. He expects vendors to deny findings until a real aircraft is shown affected, and said he would publish more tools and details later.

talks.title: 0x07: Snare - Thunderbolt and lightning, very very frightening
talks.teaser: Traces Firewire-to-Thunderbolt DMA evolution, an FPGA PCIe attack platform, macOS lock-screen bypass, and VT-d mitigation gaps.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with the lineage of direct memory access attacks over Firewire, from early framebuffer tricks through tools that patch Windows login authentication, and notes why those attacks weakened as ports vanished, addressing stayed 32-bit, and macOS began blocking DMA when FileVault and a locked screen were active. Prior Thunderbolt abuse largely chained a Firewire adapter through the exposed PCI Express tunnel, inheriting the same memory limits.

The core work explains Thunderbolt as tunneled PCI Express, then walks through an FPGA-based rig that emits transaction-layer packets over a Thunderbolt link. By spoofing a tunnel-compatible Apple SD card reader identity, the host loads a familiar driver and grants bus master. A memory write patches the locked-screen password verification path so authentication always succeeds, shown in a recorded demo on an eight-gigabyte Sandy Bridge Mac.

Closing material covers defenses: Intel VT-d DMA remapping on Ivy Bridge and later when the OS configures it, gaps on older hardware and Windows 7, and express-card equivalents. Planned follow-ons include a bus-powered miniature board, VT-d bypass research, full memory capture, kernel payload injection, and driver fuzzing via emulated devices.

talks.title: 0x07: Andreas Lindh - Attacking mobile broadband modems like a criminal
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding 0x07: Andreas Lindh - Attacking mobile broadband modems like a criminal.
talks.summary: Andreas Lindh demonstrates criminal-grade attacks against Huawei and ZTE USB modems: unauthenticated web UIs enable CSRF DNS hijacks, SMS premium-rate fraud, persistent XSS in roaming settings, and Beef-style command channels over SMS inboxes. Live demos show phishing victims through fake carrier SMS into credential harvesting, while he explains why carrier-customized firmware blocks centralized patching. Lindh urges replacing dialer-free web interfaces with authenticated clients and treating cellular dongles as permanently vulnerable Internet gateways on laptops that users rarely reboot or patch.

talks.title: 0x07: FX
talks.teaser: A keynote uses a Dune metaphor to frame who controls the internet and why firewall, detection, and patch cycles fail defenders.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by arguing that security work is framed only as winning, which hides success and punishes visible failure. He traces the internet from an early remote login crash through commercial interconnection, botnet-derived usage maps, and heavy reliance on a few centralized services, then parallels that concentration with Frank Herbert’s Dune: one scarce resource, one controller, and “great houses” that fight over it.

He sketches three modern power blocs—the global observer intelligence model, skilled ring-zero intrusion teams, and military-linked infrastructure owners—and contrasts Western mesh design with China’s centrally monitored network. Advanced persistence, high-profile destructive attacks, and vendor behavior illustrate that major players often misunderstand what they control. The middle turns to disclosure culture, from historical public shaming of slow vendors to today’s selective leaks, responsible disclosure, and commercial bug markets that erode shared knowledge. He critiques perimeter, detection, and vulnerability-scanning paradigms as mismatched to composed systems, cites hardcoded cryptography in virtual switching gear, and warns that constant patching and cloud outsourcing shift risk without fixing design.

He closes by urging practitioners to act as “natives”: think independently, resist convenience-driven trust in large providers, share workable fixes, and avoid hype that drives clumsy regulation. He points forward to a follow-on treatment of formal interface grammars for building smaller, more survivable systems.

talks.title: 2009 - Searching for Phones on the Internet
talks.teaser: Maps exposed SIP phones and PBXs across the internet, fingerprints them, and reports what a fake honeypot PBX attracted.
talks.summary:
Gauci opens with a primer on SIP, the signalling protocol behind VoIP phones and PBXs, covering its HTTP-like message format and the OPTIONS, INVITE and REGISTER methods. A single UDP probe with an OPTIONS request reveals whether an address answers as a SIP entity, which makes internet-wide scanning practical from one socket. Country sweeps sampled exposure, with Malta reported at 11.37 percent of scanned addresses replying.

To label hidden devices, he compares how each stack builds the To tag, the header order and the capitalisation of Call-ID. REGISTER scans showed that some devices return 200 OK, so strangers registered with his scanner, turning it into an accidental honeypot. A fake PBX he built then captured INVITE attempts aimed at outside numbers, some spoofing a real company, which fits toll fraud where attackers resell access to misconfigured servers. He also described digest leakage, which he estimated affects around 60 percent of endpoints in lab tests.

The takeaways are to keep PBXs off the public internet or behind a VPN, to take care with INVITE scans because they can ring real phones, and to use lockout policies for SIP authentication. He closed by discussing updates to his open source tool and a planned rewrite focused on better fingerprinting.

talks.title: 2012 - SAP Slapping
talks.teaser: A condensed guide shows how Metasploit modules expose SAP routes, weak defaults, and RFC abuse for straightforward penetration tests.
talks.summary:
Enterprise SAP landscapes combine thick clients, web portals, RFC connectors, SAProuters, and Java stacks, yet many deployments still mirror decades-old weaknesses. The presenter frames the session as internal training distilled from prior community research—especially connector-testing frameworks—and his own Metasploit modules aimed at a “zero to hero” penetration test kit rather than original vulnerability discovery.

The middle of the talk maps realistic entry paths: misconfigured SAProuters that leak state tables and proxy arbitrary traffic, cleartext or weakly protected diag and RFC credentials, default and support users across hundreds of clients, SM49/SM69-style operating-system command gadgets, hash extraction that sidesteps client isolation, and unauthenticated or loosely ACL’d remote function calls. Demos tie these ideas to lab chains such as tunneling through a router, brute-forcing clients, and riding web management consoles or host-control services to shells.

Practitioners should treat SAP like any other high-value application tier: shrink exposed connectors, assume integrators prioritized uptime over hardening, and pair network architecture review with packaged tooling so engagement time stays low. The speaker argues breaking in often remains easy while comprehensive governance and patch discipline lag, and stresses burning compromised instances rather than trusting cleanup.

talks.teaser: A skeptical tour of North Korean telecom and internet infrastructure separates rumor from evidence on cyber warfare claims.

The presentation frames North Korea as an unusually closed society whose real connectivity bears little resemblance to popular cyber-apocalypse stories. Using publicly available material, the speaker walks through domestic systems such as Kwangmyong, dial and satellite links through China and Germany, scarce internet cafés, landline and manual switching outside Pyongyang, Koryolink GSM growth, the Korean Computer Center and its overseas offices, Red Star Linux, and outsourced development arrangements. Diplomatic presences in London and Berlin illustrate how elite access to ordinary global services contrasts with restrictions on citizens.

The middle of the talk challenges influential narratives about a massive North Korean cyber military. Claims about Unit 121 and figures citing hundreds of thousands of hackers are traced to weak or anonymous sourcing, circular journalism, and commercial incentives in cyber-war training and consulting. Similar scrutiny is applied to cost models for building a foreign cyber force, political attribution of the 2009 July Fourth denial-of-service campaign, and sensational theories that lack corroboration. A lighter survey of pro-regime web properties notes outdated software, open services, and hosting concentrated outside the country.

The closing argument is that scarce resources, isolation, and ideology limit credible offensive reach more than headlines suggest. Practitioners are urged to demand attribution and evidence, treat infrastructure mapping as separate from threat hype, and weigh human-rights abuses above fear of distant server attacks.

talks.title: 2009 - Locally Exploiting Wireless Sensors
talks.teaser: Travis Goodspeed investigates 2009 - Locally Exploiting Wireless Sensors.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Travis Goodspeed presents a deep technical evaluation of the security vulnerabilities in wireless sensor network hardware and ZigBee microcontrollers, including chips widely deployed in smart electric meters, industrial monitoring, and academic sensor deployments. Addressing the common misconception that hardware acts as a secure black box or that hardware-accelerated AES-128 alone guarantees security, Goodspeed demonstrates practical physical and local attacks to extract firmware, cryptographic keys, and bypass security locks.

### Key Topics
- **Microcontroller Architecture vs. IT Security**: Embedded sensor devices lack traditional operating system defenses such as userland/kernel separation, address space layout randomization (ASLR), and dynamic linking. Code and kernel routines are statically linked, and peripherals map directly to memory addresses.
- **First-Generation ZigBee Radios**: In first-generation architectures (such as the Chipcon/TI CC2420 and Ember EM2420), radios operate as separate peripherals communicated with via synchronous serial interfaces (SPI). Cleartext AES-128 keys transmitted from the host microcontroller to the radio can be captured using physical taps (e.g., 20-gauge hypodermic needles or total phase Beagle sniffers).
- **Second-Generation SoC Vulnerabilities**: Second-generation chips integrate the radio and microcontroller onto the same die. Goodspeed reveals how both major implementations fail to protect stored keys:
  - *Ember EM250*: Incorporates an XAP2 core described in register-transfer level (RTL) code that omitted hardware protection fuses or lock bits for the JTAG/Insight interface, allowing an attacker to simply connect a debugger and dump full memory.
  - *Chipcon/TI CC2430 & CC2530*: Features an 8051 Harvard-architecture core. While a lock bit restricts JTAG commands to chip erasure, the erase command by design only purges flash memory and leaves RAM untouched. Because 8051 C compilers automatically copy constants and data from flash into data RAM at startup, erasing the flash unprotects the chip while leaving keys intact in RAM, allowing full extraction in seconds.
- **Bootloader and Glitching Attacks**: For microcontrollers such as the TI MSP430, access protection fuses and bootloader passwords can be defeated. Goodspeed presents timing attacks on bootstrap loader (BSL) password checks and explains power/voltage glitching to force instruction skipping (e.g., turning a conditional jump into a fallthrough).

### Technical Details
- **RAM Extraction & Key Recovery**: On the CC2430, dumping 8 KB of RAM reveals the 128-bit AES key (typically situated in the upper 4 KB due to power-state preservation). Using a sliding-window tool developed by Josh Wright in Python, brute-forcing the key position across RAM takes only 2 to 4 seconds.
- **Compiler Workarounds**: Storing sensitive constants in flash using compiler directives like `__code` avoids moving keys into RAM, but this breaks standard C pointer compatibility and standard library functions like `printf`.
- **Bootstrap Loader (BSL) Password Cracking**: The MSP430 bootloader password reuses the 16 interrupt vector table pointers (32 bytes total). Because unused handlers point to standard addresses or fill bytes and code aligns to even boundaries, the search space is drastically constrained. Measuring execution cycle timing differences (two cycles per correct byte match) narrows down the alphabet and allows reconstruction.
- **Voltage Glitching**: CMOS logic switching thresholds depend on supply voltage. By intentionally dipping supply voltage on specific clock edges (multiplying clock frequencies via phase-locked loops or observing power dips), attackers can cause gate-level failures that bypass fuse checks or jump instructions.

### Takeaways
- Embedded hardware cannot rely on cryptography alone; poor hardware architecture, compiler behavior, and unmaintained JTAG/bootloader interfaces completely undermine symmetric cipher security.
- Hardware issues cannot be easily patched in the field due to slim manufacturing margins, lack of over-the-air update mechanisms, and inability to recall devices.
- Mitigations include blowing hardware security fuses, randomizing interrupt vector tables to individualize BSL passwords per unit, and explicitly controlling memory placement to keep secrets out of unprotected RAM.
